prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength bring optical frequency standards to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep optical lattice clocks as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye, and my position is firmer than in round 1 because the objections raised were answered on scientific grounds rather than by counting heads. The physical idea is specific and checkable: at the magic wavelength the differential light shift of the two clock states cancels, so a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be held in a lattice and interrogated together without the trap perturbing the transition. That gives a statistical advantage that a single trapped ion does not have and a systematics programme of its own (lattice light shifts, blackbody radiation, collisions and density effects). The result has been reproduced by independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL) and, importantly for me, clock-to-clock comparisons agree at the 1e-18 level, so the uncertainty budgets have been tested against each other. It also gives access to new physics: laboratory-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on varying constants and on dark-matter couplings, and many-body spin physics in the lattice. On the chair's question about wording, I would let the citation rest on the magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms and not on 'precision' or 'accuracy' alone, because that is what separates it from the comb (2005) and from single-ion control (2012). The two-name attribution, Katori for the concept and first realisations and Ye for taking the system to the accuracy and stability frontier, is the cleanest on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is novelty: a sceptic can read lattice clocks as the next chapter of the precision-spectroscopy story that the 2005 and 2012 prizes already honoured, and ion clocks (Al+, Sr+) reach comparable accuracy by a different route. Priority at the edges is also not fully closed: Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Derevianko and Pal'chikov on the magic-wavelength theory, and the ion-clock groups lie outside the credited pair, and several of us, including me, rely on recollection of the 2001-2003 record. Finally, it is a measurement and instrument prize, not a discovery of a new state of matter, which is where my own field instinct points; I recognise that a member who prizes discovery about nature over instrument achievement can reasonably weigh this differently.

responses.point: Kroll lists the overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes as the main objection, says the committee must state the novelty carefully in the citation, and mentions the SI redefinition as a reason some might wait.
responses.response: I agree that the citation carries the weight here and have written mine so that the novelty is the magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, which the comb and ion control do not supply. On the chair's question about waiting, my position is that we should not wait. The redefinition of the second is a metrological decision taken by the CGPM on its own timetable, and its outcome does not change whether the physics was verified; the independent clock comparisons are that verification. I would, as you suggest, welcome a check by you or Lindroth against the primary record before the vote, since the priority statement is where a mistake would hurt most.

responses.point: Lindroth, who works in atomic physics, supports Katori and Ye as the clean credit, and she lists B041 (Hubbard-model quantum simulation) as her first alternative.
responses.response: Her view as the atomic physicist among us counts for more than mine on the clock record, and it reassures me that she sees the Katori and Ye split as defensible. I remain cautious about B041 as a fallback: the fermionic Hubbard simulation has not yet produced a quantitative answer that classical methods cannot, and the four-name credit would be cut to three. For this reason I would not move toward B041 even if the clock case were challenged, and I keep my own alternatives in condensed matter.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps IceCube (B012) first for Halzen and Karle as a genuine discovery of a clue from nature, grants that support is thin, and names attribution as its main weakness.
responses.response: I take the discovery argument seriously, and it is the same instinct that makes me value condensed-matter discoveries about nature. I defer to him on the neutrino physics. By the two tests I apply, independent confirmation and unambiguous credit, B012 is not yet where B007 is: the diffuse flux is confirmed but NGC 1068 is about four sigma, KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD have not yet confirmed the sources, and a two-name credit for a collaboration of hundreds with AMANDA and DUMAND precursors will be disputed. I would not oppose B012 as a later prize, and I do not think it should be a second part this year because the three-person limit would leave only one slot beside Katori and Ye and the credit there is not settled.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps fluctuation theorems (B032) first on grounds of exactness and thirty years of experimental confirmation, and concedes that priority among Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Searles, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert cannot be resolved in three names.
responses.response: I find the physics convincing and her own concession on attribution is the decisive point for me: at least seven claimants with documented results and a three-person cap would mean an unfair omission, whereas the clock credit does not. I also ask whether a theorem confirmed by experiments is a discovery in the sense of the Statutes, which she herself raises. I would revisit B032 if outside experts can propose a defensible division of the original results, but I cannot supply one from memory and will not support it this year on the present record.

responses.point: Olsson notes that the first lattice demonstration and the record accuracy are credited differently by Katori's and Ye's groups, and discloses an institutional connection to the University of Tokyo.
responses.response: I read that as supporting the pair: the claims are complementary (concept and first realisation versus accuracy, stability and many-body physics) rather than competing for the same achievement, so the two-name credit does not take from either group. I do not consider her Tokyo connection disqualifying since she reports no collaboration with the candidates, but I would keep it on the record in the committee's minutes.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as a sufficiently distinct discovery after the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which is a judgement and not a fact I can verify.
Whether Lemonde, Derevianko or Pal'chikov would have to be considered for credit; I cannot settle the 2001-2003 priority record from memory and would welcome an external check.

I do not propose a second prize part: B018 has the Metzner question and a mixed predictive record for DFT+DMFT, and B005 has an open pairing mechanism and sample dependence, so neither is a settled interpretation this year.
My knowledge of the primary clock literature and the present record uncertainties comes from recollection and has not been checked here.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no known personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye or to the other B007 names. B018 and B005 are close to my own field of electronic-structure and magnetism theory, but I do not now propose either as a prize part. I note my 2025 chairmanship only as context for my reluctance regarding B044 and have no connection to its credited names.
